entities.name: Clitomachus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Clitomachus (born Hasdrubal in 186 BCE in Carthage, died 109 BCE in Athens) was a pivotal Academic Sceptic philosopher, serving as scholarch of the Platonic Academy from 129 BCE until his death. His significance lies in his role as the primary interpreter and transmitter of the radical Sceptic doctrines of Carneades, who himself penned no works. Clitomachus bridged the intellectual traditions of the Hellenistic world, carrying Carthaginian roots to the philosophical heart of Athens and influencing subsequent Roman thought.

After his early education in Carthage, Clitomachus moved to Athens around 163 BCE, where he became a devoted student of Carneades, the founder of the Third or New Academy. He diligently recorded and systematized Carneades' complex arguments, particularly the principle of *epochē* (suspension of judgment) and the development of *pithanon* (the probable) as a guide for practical action in the absence of absolute certainty. Clitomachus authored over 400 books, though nearly all are lost, preserving Carneades' thought against dogmatic Stoic and Epicurean assertions.

Clitomachus's meticulous documentation ensured the survival and dissemination of Carneades' highly influential Sceptical arguments, which profoundly impacted later Hellenistic and Roman philosophy. His works, though fragmented, were a primary source for Roman intellectuals like Cicero, who relied on Clitomachus to articulate the Academic Sceptic position in his own philosophical dialogues, thereby shaping the intellectual landscape of the late Roman Republic. The transmission of these Sceptical methods contributed to a broader critical tradition within Western thought, questioning the foundations of knowledge.
